snapshots.name: Pericles
snapshots.body: The leading Athenian statesman as the war begins, architect of the strategy that keeps Athens supplied by sea while ceding the countryside to Spartan invasion. His funeral oration for the war's early dead becomes one of the work's most studied passages.

snapshots.name: Archidamus
snapshots.body: A king of Sparta, cautious about the war even as his city moves toward it. He commands the early Spartan invasions of Athenian territory despite his own reservations about the conflict.

snapshots.name: Themistocles
snapshots.body: An Athenian statesman from a generation earlier, hero of the Persian invasion, whose later fall from favor and exile are recalled in an extended digression. His fate serves as a cautionary backdrop to the events of the war proper.

snapshots.name: Pausanias
snapshots.body: A Spartan regent and celebrated commander from the same earlier generation as Themistocles, whose career likewise ends in disgrace. His story is told alongside Themistocles's as a companion cautionary tale.

snapshots.name: Phormio
snapshots.body: An Athenian admiral whose small squadron wins striking victories in the waters of the Corinthian Gulf. His successes there demonstrate the value of seamanship over sheer numbers.

snapshots.name: Cleon
snapshots.body: An Athenian politician who rises to prominence after Pericles's death, known for a blunt, aggressive style very different from his predecessor's. He argues forcefully for harsh measures in the debates that follow Athens's early setbacks.

snapshots.name: Diodotus
snapshots.body: An Athenian speaker who argues against Cleon in the assembly's debate over how to punish a rebellious allied city. His counterargument, based on practical consequence rather than justice, narrowly carries the day.

snapshots.name: Brasidas
snapshots.body: A Spartan general noted for boldness and diplomatic skill rare among his countrymen. His campaign in the north wins Sparta a string of allied cities away from Athens through persuasion as much as force.

snapshots.name: Nicias
snapshots.body: An Athenian general known for caution and piety, associated with the peace that briefly interrupts the war partway through. He later takes a leading, and increasingly reluctant, role in Athens's great expedition against Sicily.

snapshots.name: Demosthenes
snapshots.body: An Athenian general whose early setbacks in western Greece are followed by a notable success at Pylos. He is later sent to reinforce the faltering Athenian campaign in Sicily.

snapshots.name: Alcibiades
snapshots.body: A brilliant, controversial Athenian statesman and general, ward of Pericles, whose ambition helps drive Athens toward its expedition against Sicily. His personal enemies at home shadow his career even as he serves it abroad.

snapshots.name: Hermocrates
snapshots.body: A Syracusan statesman who argues for unity among the Sicilian Greek cities against outside interference. He becomes a leading voice in Syracuse's defense once the Athenian expedition arrives.

snapshots.name: Gylippus
snapshots.body: A Spartan commander sent to aid Syracuse against the Athenian siege. His arrival and generalship prove decisive in reversing the fortunes of the campaign in Sicily.

snapshots.name: Tissaphernes
snapshots.body: A Persian satrap governing territory along the Aegean coast, whose support becomes valuable to both Athens and Sparta as the war drags into its final phase. He plays the two sides against each other to Persia's advantage.

snapshots.name: Phrynichus
snapshots.body: An Athenian general who grows wary of Alcibiades's promises of Persian support and works against him. He becomes involved in the oligarchic movement that later shakes the Athenian constitution.

snapshots.name: Antiphon
snapshots.body: An Athenian orator regarded as the intellectual architect of the oligarchic coup that briefly overturns Athens's democracy late in the war. He works mostly behind the scenes rather than in public.

snapshots.name: Theramenes
snapshots.body: An Athenian politician involved in the oligarchic government that briefly replaces the democracy, though he grows critical of its more extreme members. His shifting position places him between the oligarchic faction and its opponents.
